## Where we landed {.smaller}

The final results, the approach behind them, and what we tested since we last met.

| Area | Where it stands |
|---|---|
| **Out-of-time forecast** *(the metric you weigh most)* | In good shape. The conversions model predicts held-out weeks at 16.1% error and the LTV model at 15.1%, both inside the 15% to 25% band these models are usually held to. The over-prediction we saw earlier has come down from every hold-out week to 4 of 13. |
| **Decisioning layer** | Live. 19 channels, the 8-column framework, sortable, with a CSV export. Meta Web is flagged low confidence, so you know which channel signal to read with caution. |
| **Baseline** | Understood, and we want to report it openly. About 67% of LTV sits in the baseline. It breaks down into genuine organic demand plus view-through credit that spend-only data can't recover. A lower number is reachable, but it carries a real cost. |
| **What we tested** | Two engines, a full sweep of the model settings, a model audit, and whether broader demand and economic signals were what the baseline was missing. The honest read is that the next gains will come from richer data more than from more modeling. |

Today is our last working session before June 4 and 5. The goals are to confirm this framing works for you and to settle the one forward data request.

---

## Out-of-time validation {.smaller}

You've said out-of-time prediction is what matters most to you for an MMM, so we want to start there. We trained on the first 79 weeks, held out the last 13 (2026-01-05 through 2026-03-30), and predicted each week against what actually happened.

| | **Model 1, Conversions** | **Model 2, LTV (3-year)** |
|---|---|---|
| MAPE | 16.13% | 15.13% |
| sMAPE | 16.41% | 13.84% |
| Signed mean error | −3.66% | +14.96% |
| Over-prediction weeks | 4 of 13 (down from 13 of 13) | 12 of 13 |
| Convergence | R-hat 1.006, ESS 1,208, 0 divergences | R-hat 1.004, ESS 2,098, 0 divergences |

Both models land inside the 15% to 25% range these models are typically held to. The conversions model used to come in high on every hold-out week, and that's now down to 4 of 13, with the average error inside plus or minus 5%.

We also want to address the concern that the intervals looked overconfident, because it's a fair one to raise. In-sample, the model's 89% interval covers 94.6% of weeks, and on the hold-out the full predictive interval covers all 13 weeks. The narrow 7.7% figure that may have stood out came from our validation report showing the band around the average prediction only. That was a reporting choice in how we displayed it, not a problem with the model.

## The decisioning layer, and which signal to read carefully {.smaller}

There are 19 channels, the 8-column framework you reviewed and approved, sortable on every column, with a CSV export so your team can slice it on their own. We'll walk through it live in a moment.

The one thing worth raising up front is that Meta Web is flagged low confidence. That isn't a hedge. It's the model being clear about where its own read is weakest, so it doesn't get over-weighted in a spend decision.

| | Meta Web |
|---|---|
| Confidence flag | Low. It doesn't pass its in-window calibration check. |
| In vs. out concentration | 1.04, essentially flat |
| What that tells us | When we tightened Meta Web's calibration, its cost level moved into range, but the model didn't change where it places the credit. |

That flat 1.04 is the signature of view-through. Meta Web earns a lot of its credit through impressions people see but don't click on, and a model that sees only spend can't place that credit on the channel. The low-confidence flag and the 1.04 are the same finding seen from two angles. The signal is genuinely uncertain, not just tied to one stretch of time.

---

## Revisiting the saturation curves {.smaller}

At our last meeting you flagged that the cost-per-acquisition curve looked flat against spend, and raised it as a possible model-validity concern. That was a fair point, and we went back and worked through it.

The first part was on our side. The curve we'd shown was the average cost per acquisition, but the spec, and your feedback, call for the marginal view, meaning the cost and return on the next dollar rather than the average across everything spent so far. We've now built the marginal curves from the existing model, with no refit needed.

The corrected marginal curve does show real curvature, which supports your read that the earlier view was masking how the model responds as spend moves. It lines up with your observation that the model wasn't capturing the variance in LTV the way you'd expect.

One thing we want to be straight about. Within the range of spend we actually observe, the curve stays close to linear. That's a genuine finding in the data, not a rendering issue. A sharp tipping point would only show up if we extrapolated well beyond the spend levels we've seen, which we'd label clearly as extrapolation, or if we imposed a stronger-saturation assumption the data doesn't support. We tried loosening that assumption, and it broke the model's convergence without revealing a tipping point, so we're not going to draw an S-curve the data doesn't show.

For the next iteration, two threads are worth carrying: whether the second engine's saturation shape surfaces a tipping point, and a closer look at why the spend-only curve stays close to linear over the range we observe. Both are good questions for after the capstone.

The corrected marginal curve is in final production for June 4 and 5, and we'll show it live on the dashboard today if it's ready by meeting time.

## The baseline, openly {.smaller}

Our model puts roughly 67% of LTV in the baseline, meaning the part that measured paid spend doesn't explain. Here is how it breaks down and the trade-off that comes with it.

| Part of the ~67% | Share | Why it's there |
|---|---|---|
| Genuine organic demand | about 35% | Customers who would subscribe without measured paid. This lines up with your read that the attributed-revenue universe is roughly two-thirds of total LTV. No spend-only model recovers it. |
| Missed paid attribution | about 32 points | Credit the model can't place on a channel, largely Meta Web view-through plus some under-instrumented channels. It lands in the baseline by default. |

A lower number is reachable, but it isn't free. We can produce a baseline near 41%, but only by loosening the link to your incrementality tests. As soon as we do that, out-of-time error rises into the mid-20s, CTV drifts off its tested value, and Meta Web's cost climbs back toward the level we spent several weeks bringing down. A 41% baseline that predicts less well and pulls the channels off calibration is a weaker result than a 67% baseline that predicts well and keeps the channels honest.

Put on the same footing as your attributed-revenue universe, the baseline works out to about 50% (a point estimate near 49.7%, in a 45% to 53% range). The distance from there to a 30% to 40% target comes down to what the data can see, not a setting we can tune.

---

## What we tested since we last met {.smaller}

We didn't stop at one model. We ran four lines of work, and each was set up to try to bring the baseline down rather than to defend it.

| Line of work | What we did | What we found |
|---|---|---|
| Two engines | Built a second, independent modeling engine on the same data. If two methods disagree, the number is an artifact of one of them. | Both land around 66% to 67%. The baseline is the same regardless of engine. (One looser setting on the second engine reaches 41%, but it gives up out-of-time accuracy and channel calibration, the same trade-off above.) |
| Model settings | Swept the levers that should move the baseline: prior tightness, the untested channels' priors, the saturation curve, the intercept prior. | None of them reaches 30% to 40% without breaking calibration. When we pushed hard toward 35%, the model settled back near 60% on its own. |
| Model audit | Tested the "overconfident intervals" concern, and tried a heavier-tailed likelihood and a hierarchical structure. | The concern turned out to be a display choice, not a model issue (94.6% in-sample coverage, full coverage on the hold-out). Neither alternative helped, and pooling actually raised the baseline. |
| Demand and macro signals | Added broader demand and economic controls to see whether the baseline was missing real outside demand. | This looked promising at first, then a closer test changed the picture. The next slide walks through it. |

The thread running through all of it is that the 67% held up across everything we tried. What's left to move it is better data more than a better setting.

---

## The demand and macro signals, in full {.smaller}

This is the one we want to walk through slowly, because it's a fair question to ask and it nearly changed our answer.

It looked promising at first. Adding a consumer-demand search index on its own brought the baseline from about 67% to 62% and improved out-of-time error from roughly 18.9% to 13.5%. When we added broader macro series, the 10-year rate and consumer sentiment, the baseline came down further to about 49%, close to the 30% to 40% range, and out-of-time error roughly halved to about 7%. On the surface, that was the result we'd been hoping to find.

Then we looked closer. Those macro series move slowly and almost in a straight line over our 93 weeks, so statistically they're hard to tell apart from a simple time trend (consumer sentiment is about 70% explained by a trend on its own). A flexible trend can look like it's explaining demand when it's really just shifting credit off the baseline, which is a re-labeling rather than a real finding.

So we ran a more careful test. We took the trend out of each macro series and re-fit on only what was left, the genuine movement that isn't just drift over time. If the macro signal were really capturing outside demand, the improvement would hold. It didn't. The baseline went back to about 62% and out-of-time error returned to about 17%.

That's why we decided not to keep it, even though it improved both headline numbers. Adopting a trend in disguise would have given us a lower baseline and a better-looking forecast, but at the cost of distorting the per-channel costs you actually make decisions on, and without reflecting any real demand the data contains. We chose to stay with the honest 67%. The model held up even against the most promising alternative we found.

## Reconciling our 67% with your other numbers {.smaller}

You've seen roughly 30% from Meridian and about 12% from Northbeam, and ours is about 67%. These aren't really in conflict. They're different tools measuring somewhat different things.

| Tool | Baseline | Why it lands there |
|---|---|---|
| Northbeam | about 12% | Uses click, view-through, and pixel-stitched journey data, which are exactly the signals we don't have. Tracking-based attribution tends to give trackable paid more credit and to miss organic. |
| Meridian | about 30% | A different set of controls and the attributed-revenue universe, which is a narrower base than total LTV. |
| Ours (MMM) | about 67% | Spend-only and privacy-durable, with no tracking. It captures the organic and offline demand that tracking misses, which tends to run higher for a subscription and credit-building business. |

The most useful read is to reconcile these rather than force them to match, since the real number likely sits between them. Tracking-based tools place credit on paid that spend-only inference can't see, and spend-only inference captures organic and word-of-mouth that tracking can't see. Pushing ours down to match a tracking tool would mean taking on that tool's blind spots. A baseline near 67% is on the high side of normal for a retention business, rather than a red flag.

---

## The forward request, the one input that moves the floor {.smaller}

Everything above points to a single, high-value data request.

Channel-level impressions or reach, especially for Meta Web.

- Why this one. Meta Web's effect works through view-through, where people see impressions and convert later without clicking. A model that sees only spend can't capture that, and it's a large part of the roughly 32 points sitting in the baseline.
- What it unlocks. Impressions are the missing signal. With them, the model can place that view-through credit on the channel directly and bring the baseline down honestly, rather than by re-labeling the way the macro test would have.
- The mechanism is already visible on our side. The flat 1.04 Meta Web concentration is the direct evidence that spend variation alone can't recover this credit. Impressions are the input that can.

This is the natural next step. You've described a roadmap of five to seven iterations, and this is what the next one would build on.

---
